table.title: The impact of social exclusion on working memory for social networks
table.research_questions:
H1a. Sociality effect: We hypothesise that individuals will classify associations from social networks more accurately and quickly than those from non-social networks. 
H1b. Self-reference effect: We hypothesise that associations from social networks that include the participant (“self-social” condition) will be classified more accurately and quickly than associations from social networks that do not include the participant (“other-social” condition).

H2a. Social exclusion effect: We hypothesise that participants who experience social exclusion (vs. inclusion) will classify associations from social networks more accurately and quickly than those from non-social networks.
H2b. Interaction between exclusion and self-relevance: We hypothesise that the effect of social exclusion on working memory performance will be strongest for self-social networks, such that participants will more accurately and quickly classify associations from self-social networks following exclusion, compared to other conditions.
H2c. Developmental moderation: We hypothesise that excluded younger participants will classify associations more accurately and quickly than excluded older participants .
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
table.study_design_overview:
This study investigates the effect of social exclusion on working memory for social networks using a mixed design. Participants will complete three behavioural tasks during a single online session. At the start of the session, participants will complete demographic questions and self-report measures assessing depressive symptoms (Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale (DASS; Lovibond & Lovibond, 1995), social sensitivity (Social Sensitivity Scale; Andrews et al., 2021) and subjective social status (McArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status, Adler et al., 2000). To assess baseline working memory capacity, participants will then complete a Digit Span task. Participants will then be randomly assigned (simple randomization) to one of two between-subject conditions in the Cyberball task (a pre-programmed ball tossing game with two other virtual players; Williams et al., 2000): social inclusion or social exclusion. In the inclusion condition, participants receive the ball equally often; in the exclusion condition, participants are initially included but are subsequently left out of the game by the other players to induce feelings of social exclusion. 
Following Cyberball, participants will complete the Network Memory Task (Andrews et al., 2024), which uses a within-subject design across three conditions: two social (1. an other-social condition and 2. a self-social condition) and a non-social condition. In the social conditions, participants read scenarios depicting fictional social interactions, either including themselves (self-social) or not (other-social). In the non-social condition, participants read scenarios depicting flight paths between cities. Participants are then tested on their memory for connections (social ties and flight paths, with accuracy and reaction time recorded. Finally, participants will complete the Reflexive and Reflective Needs Questionnaire (Williams, 2009) to assess subjective feelings of distress, belonging and motivation to reconnect directly after the Cyberball game and a second time after the Network Memory Task. The primary outcomes are accuracy and reaction time on the Network Memory Task across conditions. Data will be collected from older adolescents and adults (via Prolific).
table.randomization: Participants will be randomly assigned to either the social exclusion or inclusion condition at the participant level using block randomization within Gorilla. We will use Gorilla’s built-in randomiser to ensure each participant has an equal chance of being assigned to either condition and we will ensure approximately equal group sizes across conditions in the study. Additionally, within the Network Memory task, the order of trials and the networks shown will be randomised at the trial level to control for order effects.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures:
Adult participants will first be identified via Prolific’s internal participant pool, based on pre-screening criteria specified by the research team (e.g., age, location).  They will be approached through Prolific’s platform interface, where the study listing will appear for eligible individuals. No direct contact will occur between the research team and participants before consent is given.
Participants will be recruited through Prolific, an online platform for collecting behavioural data. Participants will be reimbursed at a rate of £9.00 per hour for their participation, as this is deemed a fair and ethical amount under the platform’s guidelines. Participants will receive £7.50 in total, as the study may take up to 50 minutes to complete. Participants will only be reimbursed if they complete the study faithfully (i.e., answer at least 3 out of the 4 attention check items correctly). 

Inclusion criteria for participants taking part in this study: 
- 18-65 years of age 
- English fluency 
- No history of head injury that caused lasting problems with memory, thinking or concentration
- No diagnosed neurological or neurodevelopmental conditions or learning disabilities
- No diagnosed psychiatric condition (except for depression and/or generalised anxiety)
table.sample_size: For this study we plan to recruit 128 adults. They will be divided into two between-subject conditions: social exclusion and social inclusion, resulting in approximately 64 participants per condition.
table.sample_size_rationale: An a priori power analysis conducted in G*Power, based on a small effect size (f = 0.15), an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power of 0.95, indicated that a total sample size of 116 participants would be required. This was informed by previous findings using the Network Memory Task with adolescents (Grunewald et al., in press), which reported a comparable effect size (f = 0.145). The analysis was designed to detect interactions among within-subject factor of condition (social-self, social-other, and non-social), as well as a between-subject factor of social inclusion vs. exclusion. Additionally, we increased the total by 10% to account for potential attrition or poor data quality in this online study, bringing the final target to 128 participants.
table.manipulated_variables:
• Social exclusion/Inclusion condition (between-subjects): Participants are randomly assigned to either an Inclusion or Exclusion condition via the Cyberball paradigm.
• Network type (within-subjects): Each participant completes trials involving both Social Networks and Non-Social Networks working memory tasks.
• Self‑Relevance (within-subjects): Within the social-network trials, participants see either self‑social networks (themselves included) or other‑social networks (they are not included).
table.measured_variables:
Self-report: 
1. Demographics: Standard demographic information will be collected including age, gender, ethnicity, and highest level of education, as well as parental education levels.
2. McArthur scale: Participants will complete the MacArthur Scale (Adler et al., 2000) to assess perceived social standing within the British society and their community.
3. Depressive symptoms. The short Depression anxiety Stress Scale (DASS-21; Lovibond & Lovibond, 1995) will be used to assess the severity of symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress over the last week on a four-point Likert scale. Every item is rated from 0 (never) to 3 (almost always) with higher scores representing higher symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress. 3
4. Social Sensitivity. The Online and Offline Social Sensitivity Scale (O2S3; Andrews et al., 2022) will be used to assess social sensitivity. It is made up of 18 items assessing sensitivity to social rejection in an online and offline context on a four-point Likert scale. The items range from 0 (strongly disagree) to 3 (strongly agree). The scale has shown to be a reliable measure of social rejection sensitivity.. 
5. The Reflexive and Reflective Questionnaire (Hales, 2009; Williams, 2009): This measure will be used to evaluate the effectiveness of the Cyberball manipulation, confirming that the exclusion and inclusion conditions elicit the intended psychological effects.

Tasks 
1. Network Memory Task accuracy: Accuracy will be identified as the correct classifications of a network connection as present vs. absent in each trial 
2. Network Memory Task reaction time: This will be the average time taken to accurately classify the associations in each condition. 
3. Backward digit span task. The standard backward digit span task will be used to compare performance on this task with the performance on the novel NMT.
table.indices:
Social 
For analyses comparing social vs non-social, social will be indexed as average performance across the social-other and social-self conditions. 

Social-self
Average accuracy and reaction time will be computed for each condition in the analyses of all hypotheses.
table.statistical_tests:
All statistical analyses will be conducted in R using linear mixed-effects models. We will run separate models for accuracy (proportion of correct response) and reaction time (RT). All models will include Participant ID as a random intercept to account for repeated measures within subjects. Age (continuous) will be included as a covariate in all models.
For Hypothesis 1a (the effect of social versus non-social condition on working memory performance), we will fit a model with Network Memory Task condition (social vs. non-social) as a fixed effect, age as a covariate, and participant ID as a random effect. We will then run a three-level model (non-social, social-other, social-self) to test specific condition differences regardless of the initial result. Hypothesis 1b (self-social networks that include the participant will be remembered more accurately than social networks that do not include the participant) will be tested within this three-level model by directly comparing self-social and other-social conditions, with pairwise comparisons to assess whether memory performance is enhanced in self-social trials.
For Hypothesis 2a (social exclusion enhances working memory for social vs. non-social networks), we extend the H1 model by adding Cyberball condition (inclusion vs. exclusion; between-subjects) and the Cyberball × Network Type (social vs. non-social; within-subjects) interaction, with age as a covariate and participant ID as a random intercept. We then mirror the follow-up used above by replacing Network Type with the three-level condition (non-social, social-other, social-self) to probe which levels drive any interaction. 
For Hypothesis 2b (social exclusion particularly enhances memory for self-social networks), we extend the H2a model by adding Cyberball condition (inclusion vs. exclusion; between-subjects) and the Cyberball × Self-relevance (self-social vs. other-social; within-subjects) interaction, with age as a covariate and participant ID as a random intercept. 
To test Hypothesis 2c whether the effect of social exclusion on memory performance varies with age, we will be examining the Cyberball × Network Type × Age interaction.

Two participants were excluded due to the absence of correct responses on the task.

Participants completed a Cyberball task inducing social inclusion or exclusion, followed by a Network Memory Task comparing social networks (i.e., relationships between people) that either included the participant (self-social/self-relevant networks) or did not include the participant (other-social/self-irrelevant networks), alongside structurally matched non-social networks (e.g., flight paths between cities).
All procedures involving human participants were performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and all relevant institutional guidelines and regulations.
A total of 128 adult participants took part in the study.
Participants were aged 18-65 years (M = 37.4, SD = 13.8).
Participants were randomly assigned to one of two between-subject conditions: social exclusion or social inclusion, with approximately equal numbers in each condition.
Informed consent was obtained electronically from all participants prior to participation.
Participants were recruited via Prolific, an online platform for behavioural research.

Age quotas were applied during recruitment to ensure a broad age distribution: approximately 35% of participants were recruited from the 18-24 age range, 35% from the 25-45 range, and the remaining 30% of participants from the 46-65 range.
Data was included in the analyses only if participants completed the study attentively, defined as correctly answering at least 3 out of 4 attention check items.
Three participants were excluded for failing pre-defined attention checks.
In line with Prolific's participant management system, rejected submissions can be replaced by new participants while maintaining the original recruitment target.

A further two participants were excluded because they did not provide any correct responses on the Backward Digit Span Task, resulting in missing baseline working memory scores required for the analyses.

One participant was excluded due to consistently below-chance task performance, and two additional participants were excluded due to missing working memory data (i.e., no correct responses on the Backward Digit Span Task).
Participants completed three behavioural tasks and selfreported measures designed to assess cognitive performance, social sensitivity, and emotional state.

At the start of the session, participants completed a demographics questionnaire, which included age, gender, ethnicity, their highest level of education and their parent's highest level of education (see Appendix B for questionnaire).

Next, participants completed the Backward Digit Span Task, a standard measure of general working memory capacity, included to enable comparisons between groups and to control for baseline cognitive ability.

Participants were instructed to indicate how much each statement applied to them over the past week using a 4-point Likert scale, ranging from 0 (did not apply to me at all / never) to 3 (applied to me very much or most of the time / always).
In this task, participants were required to recall sequences of digits in reverse order.
Following two practice trials, participants were presented with five test trials at each sequence length, beginning with two-digit sequences.
After the questionnaires and Backward Digit Span Task, participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions in the Cyberball task 18, a validated social inclusion and exclusion paradigm.
In this task participants are incorporated into a ball tossing game with two other avatars.

Participants completed self-report measures assessing subjective feelings of distress, belonging, and motivation to reconnect immediately after the Cyberball task and after the whole experiment (Reflexive and Reflective Questionnaire 49 ).
Participants were randomly assigned to either the social exclusion or social inclusion condition at the participant level using block randomisation implemented in the Gorilla Experiment Builder .
Following the Cyberball manipulation, participants completed the Network Memory Task 1, which assesses working memory for relational structures in social and non-social networks.
Following each scenario, participants were tested on their memory for network connections (i.e., social ties or flight paths), with accuracy and reaction time recorded as outcome measures.
After two practice trials, participants completed 6 trials per condition, resulting in a total of 18 trials across the task.
Within the Network Memory Task, trial order and network presentation were randomised at the trial level to control for order effects.

text.text: Humans rely on social-cognitive processes, such as social working memory, to maintain and manipulate information about social relationships.
While social and self-relevant information is often prioritised over non-social information, it remains unclear whether these processes are sensitive to social exclusion.
Therefore, this preregistered study investigated whether social exclusion influences working memory for social and non-social information.

A total of 125 participants (age: M = 37.4 years, SD = 13.8; 49.6% female) first completed Cyberball, an online task inducing feelings of social inclusion or exclusion, followed by the Network Memory Task assessing memory for social (e.g., friendship) and non-social (e.g., flight paths) networks.
Consistent with previous findings, we found that social, relative to non-social information was processed faster in working memory.
We also replicated a self-reference effect, whereby selfrelevant information was remembered more accurately and processed more quickly than nonself-relevant social and non-social information.
Contrary to our hypotheses, social exclusion did not directly impact working memory performance.
However, exploratory analyses showed that higher rejection sensitivity was associated with slower reaction times across all conditions, following exclusion.
Overall, our results suggest that the direct effects of social exclusion on working are limited and potentially dependent on individual difference in rejection sensitivity.
Humans continuously navigate complex social environments in which they must represent and update information about relationships between individuals.
The ability to maintain and manipulate social relational information in working memory, often termed social working memory, is therefore critical for effective social functioning 1, 2 .
text.formatted: The ability to maintain and manipulate social relational information in working memory, often termed social working memory, is therefore critical for effective social functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: Indeed, prior research suggests that cognitive functions have evolved to preferentially process social information, with information about our social networks processed more efficiently than structurally matched non-social information 1.
text.formatted: Indeed, prior research suggests that cognitive functions have evolved to preferentially process social information, with information about our social networks processed more efficiently than structurally matched non-social information <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref>.

text.text: Social networks refer to the interconnected relationships between individuals, such as friendships, family ties, and other stable social relationships 3 .
text.formatted: Social networks refer to the interconnected relationships between individuals, such as friendships, family ties, and other stable social relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: Unlike a group, which simply denotes a collection of individuals, a social network explicitly captures the connections between them, with people conceptualised as nodes and relationships as edges.

Efficiently representing and navigating social networks is important for social functioning, as it enables individuals to track who knows whom, understand interpersonal dynamics, and anticipate social outcomes 3 .
text.formatted: Efficiently representing and navigating social networks is important for social functioning, as it enables individuals to track who knows whom, understand interpersonal dynamics, and anticipate social outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: Working memory therefore plays a central role in social cognition by allowing individuals to temporarily retain and flexibly update relational social information 2.
text.formatted: Working memory therefore plays a central role in social cognition by allowing individuals to temporarily retain and flexibly update relational social information <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref>.

text.text: One paradigm used to examine social working memory is the Network Memory Task 1 (NMT), in which participants encode and recall relational structures that are either social (e.g., relationships between people) or non-social (e.g., flight paths between cities).
Research using this paradigm finds an overall working memory advantage for social network information.
In addition, both adults and adolescents show a self-reference effect, remembering social networks that include themselves better than networks involving others 1, 4 .
text.formatted: In addition, both adults and adolescents show a self-reference effect, remembering social networks that include themselves better than networks involving others <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: Self-referential processing, defined as the capacity to differentiate and prioritise selfrelevant over non-self-relevant information, is considered a core mechanism underlying selfrepresentational systems and the neurocognitive basis of the self 5 .
text.formatted: Self-referential processing, defined as the capacity to differentiate and prioritise selfrelevant over non-self-relevant information, is considered a core mechanism underlying selfrepresentational systems and the neurocognitive basis of the self <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that both sociality (the tendency to prioritise social vs non-social information) and self-relevance shape relational working memory performance.
Social cognition is also highly sensitive to changes in social context.
Social exclusion, defined as being ignored or rejected by others, represents a powerful social stressor that threatens the fundamental need to belong 6 .
text.formatted: Social exclusion, defined as being ignored or rejected by others, represents a powerful social stressor that threatens the fundamental need to belong <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: While much of the literature has focused on its emotional consequences, exclusion also appears to influence cognition 7 .
text.formatted: While much of the literature has focused on its emotional consequences, exclusion also appears to influence cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> .

text.text: For example, social exclusion has been associated with impaired verbal working memory and attentional filtering processes following brief virtual exclusion experiences 8, 9 .
text.formatted: For example, social exclusion has been associated with impaired verbal working memory and attentional filtering processes following brief virtual exclusion experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: In contrast, other work suggests that exclusion enhances memory for specific types of social information, particularly those related to social cues and interactions, as demonstrated in a simulated chat room experiment with undergraduate students, where rejected participants exhibited improved recall for social interactions 10 .
text.formatted: In contrast, other work suggests that exclusion enhances memory for specific types of social information, particularly those related to social cues and interactions, as demonstrated in a simulated chat room experiment with undergraduate students, where rejected participants exhibited improved recall for social interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: This pattern has been interpreted within the goal-driven resource redistribution theory 11 , which proposes that exclusion shifts cognitive attention toward socially relevant information that may support reintegration, such as social cues or relationships, while deprioritising non-social information.
text.formatted: This pattern has been interpreted within the goal-driven resource redistribution theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> , which proposes that exclusion shifts cognitive attention toward socially relevant information that may support reintegration, such as social cues or relationships, while deprioritising non-social information.

text.text: However, it remains unclear whether exclusion specifically affects working memory for social network information in the same way.
To understand why exclusion affects humans so deeply, it is important to consider the fundamental human need it threatens: the need to belong.
Humans are highly social beings, and belonging is considered a fundamental psychological need with important implications for emotional and cognitive functioning 6 .
text.formatted: Humans are highly social beings, and belonging is considered a fundamental psychological need with important implications for emotional and cognitive functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: Social connections are not only desirable, they are essential for survival and well-being, comparable in importance to basic physiological needs such as food and water 12 .
text.formatted: Social connections are not only desirable, they are essential for survival and well-being, comparable in importance to basic physiological needs such as food and water <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Supporting this view, Tomova et al. 13 found that after a brief period of social isolation, participants showed midbrain activity in regions typically associated with food craving, suggesting that the brain may encode social deprivation in a similar way to primary drives like hunger.
text.formatted: Supporting this view, Tomova et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> found that after a brief period of social isolation, participants showed midbrain activity in regions typically associated with food craving, suggesting that the brain may encode social deprivation in a similar way to primary drives like hunger.

text.text: When the need to belong is threatened through social exclusion, individuals often experience intense emotional distress, including feelings of loneliness, sadness, and anxiety 6 .
text.formatted: When the need to belong is threatened through social exclusion, individuals often experience intense emotional distress, including feelings of loneliness, sadness, and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: Importantly, exclusion is not merely distressing, it also appears to trigger compensatory mechanisms aimed at restoring social connection.
Following episodes of exclusion, individuals often show an increased motivation to reconnect with others 14 .
text.formatted: Following episodes of exclusion, individuals often show an increased motivation to reconnect with others <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> .

text.text: This drive to reconnect with others may manifest cognitively, by enhancing attention to and memory for socially relevant cues that could facilitate reintegration into the group 10, 15 .
text.formatted: This drive to reconnect with others may manifest cognitively, by enhancing attention to and memory for socially relevant cues that could facilitate reintegration into the group <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: From an evolutionary perspective, such responses may be adaptive, as maintaining social bonds increases access to protection, resources, and social support 16.
text.formatted: From an evolutionary perspective, such responses may be adaptive, as maintaining social bonds increases access to protection, resources, and social support <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref>.

text.text: Sensitivity to social exclusion may also vary across development.

Adolescents often show heightened sensitivity to peer evaluation and rejection compared to adults 17 , and prior work suggests that the cognitive and affective effects of exclusion may be particularly pronounced during adolescence 8 .
text.formatted: Adolescents often show heightened sensitivity to peer evaluation and rejection compared to adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> , and prior work suggests that the cognitive and affective effects of exclusion may be particularly pronounced during adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> .

text.text: However, it remains unclear whether age moderates the effects of exclusion on social working memory across the lifespan.
Therefore, the present study aimed to address two primary research questions: (1) How does social exclusion affect working memory for social networks?
And (2) Does this effect vary based on age, from older adolescence through adulthood?
To examine this, the study included participants aged 18-65 years, allowing investigation of potential age-related differences in sensitivity to social exclusion across adulthood.
Participants first completed the Cyberball paradigm 18 , a widely used virtual ball-tossing task designed to experimentally induce feelings of social inclusion or exclusion.
text.formatted: Participants first completed the Cyberball paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> , a widely used virtual ball-tossing task designed to experimentally induce feelings of social inclusion or exclusion.

text.text: Participants were randomly assigned to either an inclusion or exclusion condition.
Following this manipulation, participants completed the Network Memory Task 1 , in which they encoded and recalled different relational network structures.
text.formatted: Following this manipulation, participants completed the Network Memory Task <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> , in which they encoded and recalled different relational network structures.

text.text: These networks differed in content (social vs. nonsocial) and in self-relevance.
Social networks depicted relationships between people, whereas non-social networks consisted of abstract associations, such as flight paths between cities.
Additionally, social networks were either self-social (i.e., self-relevant; including the participant) or other-social (i.e., self-irrelevant; excluding the participant).
This paradigm allowed assessment of whether social exclusion influences working memory for social networks, particularly self-relevant relational information.

Based on prior literature, a social prioritisation effect (H1a) was hypothesised, such that participants would classify associations from social networks more accurately and more quickly than associations from non-social networks.

A self-reference effect (H1b) was also hypothesised, whereby participants would classify associations from self-social networks (i.e., networks that include themselves) more accurately and more quickly than associations from other-social networks (i.e., networks that do not include themselves).
With regard to social exclusion, it was hypothesised that excluded participants would show enhanced performance for social relative to non-social networks (H2a).

In addition, exclusion effects were expected to be strongest for self-social networks (H2b), such that excluded participants would classify associations from self-social networks more accurately and more quickly than in other conditions.
Finally, age was examined as a potential moderator of exclusion effects (H2c), with younger participants hypothesised to show stronger exclusionrelated effects than older participants.

Together, these hypotheses aimed to clarify how sociality, self-relevance, and exclusion interact with age to shape social working memory, providing insight into the cognitive mechanisms underlying social development.

Human cognition is deeply embedded in social environments, where the ability to represent and remember relationships between individuals is important for effective social functioning.
As social exclusion threatens a fundamental need to belong, it may shape how such social information is processed and remembered.
Therefore, the present study examined whether social and self-relevant information is prioritised in working memory and whether this prioritisation is influenced by social exclusion.

Participants completed a Cyberball task inducing social inclusion or exclusion, followed by a Network Memory Task comparing social networks (i.e., relationships between people) that either included the participant (self-social/self-relevant networks) or did not include the participant (other-social/self-irrelevant networks), alongside structurally matched non-social networks (e.g., flight paths between cities).
Five main findings emerged.
First, social information was processed more efficiently than non-social information, reflected in faster reaction times.
Second, self-relevant networks showed a robust processing advantage, with faster and more accurate performance.
Third, social exclusion did not influence working memory performance or the prioritisation of social, self-social, or other-social network information.
Fourth, exploratory analyses suggested that rejection sensitivity moderated cognitive responses to exclusion, indicating that stable individual differences may influence exclusion-related effects.
Finally, these effects were not moderated by age.
However, exploratory analyses indicated that trait level rejection sensitivity might interact with exclusion experiences to impact domain general working memory performance.
Consistent with prior work using the Network Memory Task 1, 4 , participants responded faster to social compared with non-social networks.
text.formatted: Consistent with prior work using the Network Memory Task <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> , participants responded faster to social compared with non-social networks.

text.text: Although accuracy did not differ significantly across conditions, this likely reflected ceiling effects, as overall performance was high.
These findings support the prior evidence suggesting that social information is prioritised in cognition and processed more efficiently than comparable non-social information.
For example, similar social prioritisation effects have been observed across attention, memory, and perception paradigms [19] [20] [21].
text.formatted: For example, similar social prioritisation effects have been observed across attention, memory, and perception paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>.

text.text: One explanation for this advantage is that human cognition evolved to efficiently process social relationships and group dynamics 22 .
text.formatted: One explanation for this advantage is that human cognition evolved to efficiently process social relationships and group dynamics <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> .

text.text: Supporting this account, individual differences in social working memory have been found to be associated with real-world social network size 23 .
text.formatted: Supporting this account, individual differences in social working memory have been found to be associated with real-world social network size <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> .

text.text: Social information may also receive processing priority because it serves an important functional role in everyday life.

Efficiently representing social relationships allows individuals to track interpersonal connections, anticipate social outcomes, and navigate complex social environments 24 Alternatively, the advantage may partly reflect greater familiarity with social relational structures compared to abstract non-social networks.
text.formatted: Efficiently representing social relationships allows individuals to track interpersonal connections, anticipate social outcomes, and navigate complex social environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> Alternatively, the advantage may partly reflect greater familiarity with social relational structures compared to abstract non-social networks.

text.text: Repeated exposure to social interactions throughout life may facilitate more efficient encoding of social information.
However, because the task involved learning novel networks, familiarity alone is unlikely to fully explain the observed advantage.
Therefore, social prioritisation likely reflects a combination of evolutionary pressure, functional relevance, and experiential familiarity.
Our study also demonstrated a self-reference effect in working memory.
Participants responded faster and more accurately when processing self-social networks compared to other-social or non-social networks.
This finding is consistent with extensive evidence showing that self-relevant information is encoded and remembered more efficiently than nonself-relevant information 25, 26 .
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with extensive evidence showing that self-relevant information is encoded and remembered more efficiently than nonself-relevant information <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> .

text.text: Moreover, self-relevant stimuli capture attention even under minimal processing conditions, indicating a general prioritisation mechanism that facilitates encoding and retrieval 27 .
text.formatted: Moreover, self-relevant stimuli capture attention even under minimal processing conditions, indicating a general prioritisation mechanism that facilitates encoding and retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> .

text.text: Importantly, the present findings extend this effect to relational working memory, suggesting that self-relevance enhances the encoding and retrieval of associations between network structures.
A central explanation for this effect is that self-relevant information is integrated within a rich and well-organised self-schema.
According to this account, the self provides a highly structured knowledge system that supports deeper encoding, richer associations, and more efficient retrieval 25, 28 .
text.formatted: According to this account, the self provides a highly structured knowledge system that supports deeper encoding, richer associations, and more efficient retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> .

text.text: This increases the number of available retrieval pathways and facilitates memory performance.

This interpretation is further supported by evidence that selfreferential processing emerges early in development, with infants as young as 18 months showing enhanced memory for self-associated objects in tasks requiring them to distinguish between objects belonging to themselves and those belonging to a puppet 29 .
text.formatted: This interpretation is further supported by evidence that selfreferential processing emerges early in development, with infants as young as 18 months showing enhanced memory for self-associated objects in tasks requiring them to distinguish between objects belonging to themselves and those belonging to a puppet <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> .

text.text: Complementing this, self-reference may also enhance cognitive 'binding' processes, facilitating integration across elements and processing stages 30 .
text.formatted: Complementing this, self-reference may also enhance cognitive 'binding' processes, facilitating integration across elements and processing stages <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> .

text.text: Rather than reflecting a distinct mechanism, this account specifies how self-relevance enhances cognitive performance by promoting more efficient integration within working memory.
In the present task, this likely supported the formation of more coherent relational representations, improving both encoding and retrieval.

This effect is likely to be particularly adaptive in real-world settings, where tracking one's position within a social network is essential for maintaining relationships, anticipating others' behaviour, and navigating complex social environments.
Contrary to our hypotheses, social exclusion did not influence working memory performance or modulate prioritisation of social, self-social, or other-social network information.

This contrasts with prior work suggesting that exclusion either impairs cognitive performance through resource depletion 7, 9, 31, 32 or enhances attention to social information to facilitate reconnection 10, 11, 33 .

text.text: However, null effects are rarely reported in the literature, with only limited evidence suggesting an absence of exclusion effects, particularly in adult samples 8 .
text.formatted: However, null effects are rarely reported in the literature, with only limited evidence suggesting an absence of exclusion effects, particularly in adult samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> .

text.text: This suggests that while effects of social exclusion are often found, they may not be uniformly observed across all populations and paradigms.

One interpretation of our lack of effects, is that social and self-referential prioritisation reflects relatively stable properties of cognitive processing that are not easily altered by transient social experiences.
From this perspective, prioritisation effects observed in working memory may reflect enduring domain-sensitive biases rather than flexible, state-dependent shifts in cognitive allocation 34, 35 .
text.formatted: From this perspective, prioritisation effects observed in working memory may reflect enduring domain-sensitive biases rather than flexible, state-dependent shifts in cognitive allocation <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> .

text.text: This interpretation is consistent with the overall pattern of results observed in the present study, in which social and self-relevant information was prioritised irrespective of exclusion condition.
Crucially, this suggests that while exclusion may influence motivation or affective processes, it does not necessarily extend into higherlevel cognitive systems involved in relational integration.
Alternatively, exclusion effects may depend on task demands.

Prior studies often employed relatively simple paradigms 9 , whereas the present task required encoding and retrieval of complex relational structures, placing greater demands on working memory and cognitive control.
text.formatted: Prior studies often employed relatively simple paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> , whereas the present task required encoding and retrieval of complex relational structures, placing greater demands on working memory and cognitive control.

text.text: Under these conditions, exclusion-related motivational shifts may have less influence on performance.
This interpretation aligns with broader evidence suggesting that higher cognitive load can limit the extent to which motivational or affective factors influence cognitive processing 36, 37 .
text.formatted: This interpretation aligns with broader evidence suggesting that higher cognitive load can limit the extent to which motivational or affective factors influence cognitive processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref> .

text.text: Together, the findings suggest that the cognitive effects of social exclusion may be constrained by task complexity and cognitive demands, highlighting important boundary conditions for exclusion effects in working memory.
Thus, exclusion-related effects may primarily emerge in tasks that allow flexible attentional allocation but are reduced when performance is constrained by high cognitive demands.
Although no overall effects of social exclusion were observed, exploratory analyses suggested that stable individual differences may influence cognitive responses to exclusion.
Specifically, individuals reporting higher rejection sensitivity showed slower reaction times following exclusion than inclusion.
This suggests that the cognitive impact of exclusion varies across individuals.

One explanation is that rejection-sensitive individuals continue to cognitively and emotionally process the exclusion experience during the subsequent task, reducing cognitive efficiency and slowing responses.

This interpretation is consistent with cognitive resource and affective interference accounts 36, 37 and with evidence showing prolonged emotional responses to exclusion in socially sensitive individuals 38 .
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with cognitive resource and affective interference accounts <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref> and with evidence showing prolonged emotional responses to exclusion in socially sensitive individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> .

text.text: Importantly, rejection sensitivity reflects a broader trait disposition characterised by heightened expectations of rejection, emotional reactivity, and reduced cognitive efficiency under stress 36, 39 , rather than immediate responsiveness to experimentally induced exclusion alone.
text.formatted: Importantly, rejection sensitivity reflects a broader trait disposition characterised by heightened expectations of rejection, emotional reactivity, and reduced cognitive efficiency under stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39</ref> , rather than immediate responsiveness to experimentally induced exclusion alone.

text.text: Individuals higher in rejection sensitivity may therefore experience exclusion as more salient and carry its effects into subsequent cognitive processing.
Together, these findings suggest that stable individual differences, rather than transient social experiences alone, may partly determine the cognitive consequences of social exclusion.
In contrast, the present study found no evidence that age moderated the effects of social exclusion on working memory performance.

Although adolescence is often characterised as a period of heightened sensitivity to social evaluation 17 , exclusion effects may be strongest in earlier developmental periods (approximately ages 10-14) 8 , which were not represented in the present sample.
text.formatted: Although adolescence is often characterised as a period of heightened sensitivity to social evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> , exclusion effects may be strongest in earlier developmental periods (approximately ages 10-14) <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> , which were not represented in the present sample.

text.text: Age did, however, consistently predict slower reaction times, consistent with established age-related declines in processing speed 40, 41 .
text.formatted: Age did, however, consistently predict slower reaction times, consistent with established age-related declines in processing speed <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> .

text.text: Importantly, this effect was independent of social content and exclusion condition, suggesting domain-general cognitive slowing rather than changes in social prioritisation.
Our results should be considered within the context of a number of limitations.
First, the effects of the Cyberball manipulation may have attenuated over time.

Although participants reported clear feelings of exclusion immediately following the task, these effects were reduced in later reflective ratings, suggesting that the emotional impact of exclusion may not have been sustained throughout the experiment.
This attenuation may have been amplified by the online testing environment, where participant engagement and immersion are more difficult to control.
Second, accuracy performance showed evidence of ceiling effects, likely due to the use of low-load stimuli in the Network Memory Task.

Although low-load conditions were selected based on prior work demonstrating stronger social processing effects under reduced cognitive demand 1 , this may have limited sensitivity to detect subtle condition differences in accuracy.
Whilst primary analyses were hypothesis-driven and preregistered, exploratory findings should be interpreted cautiously and need to be replicated in larger samples.
Future research should examine whether exclusion more strongly influences social working memory earlier in adolescence, when sensitivity to peer evaluation is heightened.

Indeed, developmental research suggests that concerns about peer acceptance peak in midadolescence (around ages 15-16) and decline thereafter, alongside a peak in social anxiety and the onset of social anxiety during this period 42, 43 .
text.formatted: Indeed, developmental research suggests that concerns about peer acceptance peak in midadolescence (around ages 15-16) and decline thereafter, alongside a peak in social anxiety and the onset of social anxiety during this period <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43</ref> .

text.text: Therefore, replication in a younger age sample may elucidate developmental responses to exclusion that the current study is unable to examine.

It may also be valuable to investigate how real-world social factors, including loneliness, friendship quality, and social network size, relate to relational working memory under conditions of exclusion.
For example, it is possible that individuals with close, supportive, friendships may buffer against the effects of short-term induced exclusion.
Finally, future studies should examine whether exclusion differentially affects processing of emotionally valenced social information, such as affiliative or threatening social cues.

This is because prior research suggests that negative social information may be preferentially processed within social networks 44 , raising the possibility that exclusion selectively alters attention to threat-related or affiliative social cues.
text.formatted: This is because prior research suggests that negative social information may be preferentially processed within social networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> , raising the possibility that exclusion selectively alters attention to threat-related or affiliative social cues.

text.text: Overall, the present study replicates previous work demonstrating that social network information is prioritised in working memory, relative to non-social networks.
This was reflected in faster processing of social networks and enhanced performance for self-relevant associations.
Social exclusion did not influence working memory performance or modulate the prioritisation of social information.

However, exploratory results offer important avenues for future work, suggesting that trait-levels of rejection sensitivity may interact with exclusion experiences to impact working memory performance.

In summary, these findings suggest that social and self-referential prioritisation in working memory may reflect relatively stable features of cognitive processing rather than flexible responses to short-term social experiences, such as social exclusion.

text.text: All procedures involving human participants were performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and all relevant institutional guidelines and regulations.
A total of 128 adult participants took part in the study.
Participants were aged 18-65 years (M = 37.4, SD = 13.8).
The sample included 64 females, 63 males, and 1 participant who identified as another gender or preferred not to say.
The sample size was based on an a priori power analysis conducted in G*Power 3.1.9.7 45 , assuming a small effect size (f = 0.15), α = 0.05, and power = 0.95.

text.text: This was informed by previous findings using the Network Memory Task with adolescents 4 , which reported a comparable effect size (f = 0.145).
Additionally, we increased the total by 10% to account for potential attrition or poor data quality in this online study, bringing the final target to 128 participants.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of two between-subject conditions: social exclusion or social inclusion, with approximately equal numbers in each condition.

Participants taking part in this study had to be 18-65 years old, fluent in English, and have no history of head injury that caused lasting problems with memory, thinking, or concentration, no diagnosed neurological or neurodevelopmental conditions or learning disabilities, and no diagnosed psychiatric condition (except for depression and/or generalised anxiety).
Informed consent was obtained electronically from all participants prior to participation.
Participants were recruited via Prolific, an online platform for behavioural research.

Age quotas were applied during recruitment to ensure a broad age distribution: approximately 35% of participants were recruited from the 18-24 age range, 35% from the 25-45 range, and the remaining 30% of participants from the 46-65 range.
Participants received £6.75 for completing the approximately 50-minute-long study.
Data was included in the analyses only if participants completed the study attentively, defined as correctly answering at least 3 out of 4 attention check items.
Three participants were excluded for failing pre-defined attention checks.
In line with Prolific's participant management system, rejected submissions can be replaced by new participants while maintaining the original recruitment target.
Consequently, the final sample size reflects the planned number of valid cases.
Additionally, one participant was excluded due to consistently below-chance accuracy across all task conditions, indicating a failure to adequately understand the task.

A further two participants were excluded because they did not provide any correct responses on the Backward Digit Span Task, resulting in missing baseline working memory scores required for the analyses.
Following these exclusions, the final sample comprised 125 participants, with n = 62 in the Exclusion and n = 63 in the Inclusion condition.

text.text: The DASS-21 is a self-report questionnaire consisting of three 7item subscales measuring depression, anxiety, and stress.

Participants were instructed to indicate how much each statement applied to them over the past week using a 4-point Likert scale, ranging from 0 (did not apply to me at all / never) to 3 (applied to me very much or most of the time / always).

text.text: The 18-item measure assesses sensitivity to social evaluation and interpersonal experiences in both online and offline contexts.

Participants rated their agreement with statements describing feelings in social situations on a 4-point Likert scale (0 = strongly disagree,3 = strongly agree), with higher scores indicating greater social sensitivity.
Internal consistency was good (Cronbach's α = 0.91).
General working memory capacity was measured using the Backward Digit Span Task, a standardised measure of working memory.
In this task, participants were required to recall sequences of digits in reverse order.
Following two practice trials, participants were presented with five test trials at each sequence length, beginning with two-digit sequences.
Advancement to the next level required correct recall on at least three of the five trials.
Sequence length increased by one digit at each level (e.g., from two to three digits), and the task continued until participants failed to meet the performance criterion at a given level.

text.text: Participants rated the extent to which their basic social need to belong and their mood were threatened during the game.
Each questionnaire included three items assessing belonging, with two items reverse-coded.
Responses were provided on Likert scales, with higher scores indicating greater perceived need threat and stronger feelings of exclusion.

Although the full questionnaires are considerably longer, for the purposes of this study the focus was only on the first three items assessing belonging, the mood items (happy and sad), and the manipulation check items measuring perceived exclusion and the proportion of times participants believed they received the ball (see Appendix B for full item list).
Internal consistency was good in the present sample (RXQ Belonging α = 0.93; RCQ Belonging α = 0.87).
After the questionnaires and Backward Digit Span Task, participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions in the Cyberball task 18 , a validated social inclusion and exclusion paradigm.
text.formatted: After the questionnaires and Backward Digit Span Task, participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions in the Cyberball task <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> , a validated social inclusion and exclusion paradigm.

text.text: In this task participants are incorporated into a ball tossing game with two other avatars.

In the inclusion condition, participants received the ball equally throughout the game (1/3 out of all the 30 throws); in the exclusion condition, they initially received the ball but then were subsequently left out of the game by the two other avatars (they receive the ball twice in the beginning and then not anymore).
This manipulation is designed to induce feelings of social inclusion or exclusion.

Participants completed self-report measures assessing subjective feelings of distress, belonging, and motivation to reconnect immediately after the Cyberball task and after the whole experiment (Reflexive and Reflective Questionnaire 49 ).

text.text: Participants were randomly assigned to either the social exclusion or social inclusion condition at the participant level using block randomisation implemented in the Gorilla Experiment Builder .
Gorilla's built-in randomiser ensured equal probability of assignment and approximately balanced group sizes across conditions.
Following the Cyberball manipulation, participants completed the Network Memory Task 1 , which assesses working memory for relational structures in social and non-social networks.
The task employed a within-subject design with three conditions: two social conditions (selfsocial and other-social) and one non-social condition.
For timing reasons, only the low-load condition from Andrews et al. 1 was used.
text.formatted: For timing reasons, only the low-load condition from Andrews et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> was used.

text.text: This was chosen because in previous work the low-load (3 nodes per network), relative to the high-load (4 nodes per network), condition generated the most reliable effects.
That is, in the low-load condition, networks consisted of three individuals (in the social conditions) or three cities (in the non-social condition), rather than four.
In the social conditions, participants read short scenarios describing fictional social interactions, either involving themselves (self-social) or involving others only (other-social).
In the non-social condition, participants read scenarios describing flight connections between cities.
Following each scenario, participants were tested on their memory for network connections (i.e., social ties or flight paths), with accuracy and reaction time recorded as outcome measures.
After two practice trials, participants completed 6 trials per condition, resulting in a total of 18 trials across the task.

All statistical analyses were conducted in R using linear mixed-effects models.
Separate models for accuracy (proportion of correct response) and reaction time (RT for correct trials only) were run.
All models included Participant ID as a random intercept to account for repeated measures within subjects.
Age (continuous) was included as a covariate in all models.

For Hypothesis 1a (the effect of social versus non-social condition on working memory performance), a model with Network Memory Task condition (social vs. non-social) as a fixed effect, age as a covariate, and participant ID as a random effect was fitted.
Afterwards, a three-level model (non-social, social-other, social-self) was run to test specific condition differences regardless of the initial result.

Hypothesis 1b (self-social networks that include the participant will be remembered more accurately than social networks that do not include the participant) was tested within this three-level model by directly comparing self-social and other-social conditions, with pairwise comparisons to assess whether memory performance is enhanced in self-social trials.

For Hypothesis 2a (social exclusion enhances working memory for social vs. non-social networks), the H1 model was extended by adding Cyberball condition (inclusion vs. exclusion; between-subjects) and the Cyberball × Network Type (social vs. non-social; within-subjects) interaction, with age as a covariate and participant ID as a random intercept.
The follow-up used above was mirrored by replacing Network Type with the three-level condition (non-social, social-other, social-self) to probe which levels drive an interaction.

For Hypothesis 2b (social exclusion particularly enhances memory for self-social networks), the H2a model was extended by adding Cyberball condition (inclusion vs. exclusion; between-subjects) and the Cyberball × Self-relevance (self-social vs. other-social; withinsubjects) interaction, with age as a covariate and participant ID as a random intercept.
To test Hypothesis 2c (the effect of social exclusion on memory performance varies with age) the Cyberball x Age and the Cyberball × Network Type × Age interaction was examined.

Figure 1: Reaction time for social vs non-social networks.
Points represent individual participants' mean reaction times per condition (N = 125).
Boxplots display the median and interquartile range, and density distributions illustrate the distribution of responses.
Nonsocial networks consisted of abstract items without social content (e.g., flight patterns), and social networks included social components.
Reaction time reflects the mean response time for correct trials only.
Participants responded significantly faster to social compared to nonsocial networks (≈110 ms difference), indicating more efficient processing of social information.
Error bars reflect standard errors.
Figure 2: Self-reference advantage in working memory for social networks.
Panel (left) shows mean accuracy for each network type (non-social, other-social, self-social), and panel (right) shows corresponding mean reaction times.
Individual participant data ( N = 125) points are displayed alongside boxplots and rainclouds.
Non-social networks: flight patterns between cities, Other-social networks: networks including other people but not the participant, Selfsocial networks: networks including the participant.
Accuracy was defined as the proportion of correctly recalled trials.
Reaction time was defined as the average response time on correct trials.
Error bars represent ±1 SE.
